explanation: Mixture: fires on tokens right after a contrast or negation that signals difficulty or obstruction ('However[[,]]', 'difficult[[ to]]', 'doesn[['t]]', 'there is[[ no]]', 'prevents', 'avoid', 'may not[[ be]]'), and separately on 'Ju'/'jue'-type name and month fragments ('[[ju]]in', 'jueves', 'Juan', 'Juergensen'). Neutral text gives little or nothing.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, mostly in non-English Latin-script text (Spanish/Portuguese/French/German/Czech/Norwegian: 'P'ero, 'bus'quem, 'sup'prime, 'encour'ager) and in rare English or technical words ('chem[[op]]rotective', ' tre'asured, ' c'uffed). Weak on whole common English words.

Fires on parts of file paths, URLs, module/require names and include-guard or header names in code (public[[_html]], r[[uby]].exe, '= require(', _HPP, '#include <', /master, /latest), i.e. tokens that name files, directories or package paths. Prose gives little.

Fires on tokens inside sports-statistics and sports-description text: stat abbreviations and numbers ('GAA =', '.535', '14 points'), position words ('left back', 'plays as a'), 'power-play', 'offensive rebounds', 'led the league in'. It also fires weakly-to-moderately on video-game genre and description text. Non-sports text gives little.

Fires on the word stem 'press' in any sense: physical pressure ('blood pressure', 'high pressure', 'pressurized'), pressing a button or key, pressing someone or pressing ahead (political pressure), and 'the press' / 'press briefing' / French 'pression' and 'presse'. Related words (pump, push, compressed air) and the letters 'Pres' in 'Presiding' give weak activation.

Loosely fires on words about relations between two things, such as substitution, opposition, complement or mutual action ('complement or[[ substitute]]', 'into[[ another]]', 'each[[ other]]', 'opposite', 'interactive', 'opposed', 'interference'). It also fires on middle pieces of chemistry or biomedical words ('hydro[[ly]]sis', 'sup[[ram]]olecular', 'potent[[iate]]', 'est'er). The two groups seem unrelated.

Fires on words about continuation or keeping something unchanged: 'remain', 'still', 'continue to', 'retain', 'keep', 'stay intact', 'be able to', 'keep the same'. This includes the token after 'must retain' in license text ('retain[[ the]] above copyright'). Fires most on the continuation word itself or the token right after it.

Fires on citation and reference formatting tokens: 'et[[ al]]', reference markers like '[@B10]' and their digits, legal citation parentheses and years, and disambiguation parentheses after names in wiki lists ('Liu Shan[[ (]]', 'David[[ (]]surname)'). Ordinary prose gives little.

Fires on a clause-linking connective that introduces a purpose or consequence after a stated situation: ', so (that)', 'hence', 'thus', 'to' meaning 'in order to', and to a lesser degree 'and' joining a follow-on clause. Strongest on 'so' after a description of a goal or setup.

Fires mainly inside HTTP-request code and configuration: the indentation before keys in jQuery $.ajax option objects (url, cache, success), 'Content-type' and 'MIME' headers, 'new' in credential setup, OAuth URLs and Apache config lines. It also fires weakly on the second part of some person or place names ('Fabien Pot'encier, 'Mag'dalene).

Hard to pin down. Fires on the first piece of a rare proper name or technical term split into subwords ('tet'raethylammonium, 'No'oreyezdan, 'Hy'aluronic, 'Co'chrane, 'Co'aker, 'Deg'enaar, 'nucle'otides), often after a list or a preceding name. It also fires on scattered punctuation and numbers in drug/dose lists and in URLs. Not predictable from one feature.

No common feature. Fires strongly on a heterogeneous set: chemistry notation (C=C, '-free', chemical formula pieces, 'transesterification'), the 'District' in court names, code keywords and attributes (nonatomic, const, 'fa fa-', regex), Markdown separators ('======'), and LaTeX pieces. Hard to predict.

A mixture: 'into' after 'randomized/divided' in study-design text, the '-' in 'Let x = a - b' arithmetic problems, 'AS IS' in license text, and many other unrelated tokens completing set phrases ('This file is[[ part]]', 'does what it[[ says]]', 'successful[[ run]]'). There is no single shared feature.

Mainly fires on polynomial terms in auto-generated algebra problems ('Let f(x) = x**3 - 7*x**[[2]] + 6*x'): the exponent '2' after '**' and the '*x' coefficient-variable pieces. It is weaker and scattered on other technical tokens ('coefficients of determination', 'potentiation', 'inverse', 'first order').
